# The Grocery AP Automation Benchmark Report: Summer 2026 Edition


**by Mike Waldron**


**Why This Report Exists**


Independent and regional grocers have always operated on margins that don’t forgive much. A fraction of a percent is the difference between a profitable quarter and a loss, which means a UNFI invoice with 15 incorrect line items, or a DSD vendor who’s been quietly creeping prices for three months, isn’t an administrative nuisance. It’s a margin problem.


Most operators know this. What they don’t have is the data to quantify it: to walk into a vendor conversation and say, here’s exactly what you overbilled us, here’s the credit we’re owed, here’s the pattern we’ve been seeing. That gap between knowing something is wrong and proving it is where grocery AP has always struggled.


We process hundreds of thousands of invoices every quarter across our grocery customer base. This report is what that data actually shows, not industry estimates, not survey responses, but numbers pulled from real operations.


This is the first edition. Twice a year, we’ll track how these numbers move, flag what’s driving the changes, and give grocers a benchmark they can actually use. This edition covers overcharges, fraud exposure, discrepancy rates, payment errors, invoice lifecycle time, and AP labor savings.


## Profitability Benchmarks


### Overcharges


**Benchmark** : The typical grocer is overcharged an average of $37,611 per location per year.


In Spring 2026 alone, Ottimate already uncovered $1.87 million in overcharges, on pace to significantly outperform the $4.25 million annualized benchmark. Per location, the typical customer uncovered $9,417 in that same period.


Here’s the thing about vendor overcharges: they don’t show up as a line item called “billing error.” They hide in price creep, in catch weight variances, in DSD slips that nobody had time to reconcile. For a multi-store operator without automated overcharge detection, $37,000 per location is quietly leaving every year across all locations.


### Invoice Risk


**Benchmark** : 55 percent of grocers reported experiencing invoice fraud or overpayment in the past year.


So far in 2026, 75 percent of grocery accounts had at least one invoice flagged for potential risk. The average flagged invoice carried $3,595 in exposure.


That number, 75 percent, is worth sitting with. Three out of four accounts. The question for any grocer not using automated flagging isn’t whether risky invoices are getting through. It’s how many, and at what cost.


### Invoice Discrepancies


**Benchmark** : 26 percent of invoices matched to a receiving document have at least one discrepancy. Price mismatches account for 76 percent of all discrepancy line items.


This year, 77 percent of grocery invoices linked to a receiving document had at least one active discrepancy. Roughly 63 percent were flagged for price variance.


This is the penny gap at scale. At nearly 10,000 invoices per account per quarter, a header-level review catches the obvious stuff, a wrong total, a duplicate invoice. It misses the line items: the case of chicken breast billed at last week’s price instead of this week’s contract price, the KeHE mispick that got received and coded but never disputed. Item-level validation isn’t optional in grocery. It’s where the margin actually lives.


### Payments


**Benchmark** : Ottimate caught 14,250 payments with errors last year, accounting for $1.6 million in potential losses.


Through the first half of 2026, Ottimate has already caught 6,026 payments with errors, $1.01 million in potential losses before funds left the account.


Once a payment goes out, recovering it means chasing a credit memo from a vendor who has every incentive to be slow about it. The operators who catch errors before disbursement aren’t just saving money. They’re avoiding a process that’s slow, frustrating, and often unsuccessful.


## Productivity Benchmarks


### Invoice Lifecycle Time


**Benchmark** : Grocery customers have reduced invoice lifecycle time from three days to under one day, saving the average account $264,000 per year in AP labor.


This summer, the average invoice lifecycle is 34.3 hours, slightly above the sub-24-hour benchmark. But 70.2 percent of grocery invoices are getting approved the same day, and Q2 2026 customers saved an estimated $70,000 per account in AP labor from faster processing.


Getting from three days to one day is a configuration problem before it’s a performance problem. Approval workflows need to be built, vendors need to be mapped, the manual handoffs need to come out. The operators who’ve done that work are processing nearly 10,000 invoices a quarter with their AP team spending time on exceptions, disputes, vendor calls, coding edge cases, instead of routine review.


### AP Labor Savings


**Benchmark** : Ottimate codes 93.3 percent of line items to the correct GL automatically, saving customers an average of 106 hours per month.


In 2026, Ottimate is coding 94.9 percent of grocery line items to the correct GL without anyone touching them. The typical grocery account is getting back 182 hours of GL coding labor per month.


For a one- or two-person AP operation, which describes most independent grocers, 182 hours is a different job description. That’s the AP clerk who’s no longer the human scanner, manually keying data that’s already digital. It’s the controller who closes the month without a week of cleanup first.


## About This Report


The Grocery AP Automation Quarterly Trends Report is published by Ottimate using aggregated, anonymized data from our grocery customer base. All benchmarks reflect real invoice processing data across independent and regional grocery operators. This is the first edition; future editions will track trends and flag what’s driving the changes.
